evidence.claim: A mostly gravel crossing that first brought road travelers to Denali National Park.
evidence.quote: Denali Highway (Alaska Route 8) is a lightly traveled, mostly gravel highway in the U.S. state of Alaska. It leads from Paxson on the Richardson Highway to Cantwell on the Parks Highway. Opened in 1957, it was the first road access to Denali National Park.

evidence.claim: The Denali Highway climbs steeply from Paxson into the foothills of the central Alaska Range, then winds through the Amphitheater Mountains.
evidence.quote: Traveling west, the Denali Highway leaves the Richardson Highway (Alaska Route 4) at Paxson, and climbs steeply up into the foothills of the central Alaska Range.

evidence.claim: The Denali Highway climbs steeply from Paxson into the foothills of the central Alaska Range, then winds through the Amphitheater Mountains.
evidence.quote: The first 45 miles (72 km) winds through the Amphitheater Mountains

evidence.claim: Most of its 135 miles are gravel.
evidence.quote: The Denali Highway is 135 miles (217 km) in length.

evidence.claim: Most of its 135 miles are gravel.
evidence.quote: a lightly traveled, mostly gravel highway

evidence.claim: Washboarding and dust are common; in good weather, the route offers views of the Alaska Range’s peaks and glaciers.
evidence.quote: Washboarding and extreme dust are common

evidence.claim: Washboarding and dust are common; in good weather, the route offers views of the Alaska Range’s peaks and glaciers.
evidence.quote: Along the way, in good weather, there are views of the peaks and glaciers of the central Alaska Range

evidence.claim: The first 21 miles, reaching Tangle Lakes, are paved.
evidence.quote: The first 21 miles (34 km), to Tangle Lakes, are paved.

evidence.claim: Alaska residents pressed for road access to Denali National Park in the early 1930s, after the Alaska Railroad’s construction in 1923.
evidence.quote: Following the construction of the Alaska Railroad in 1923, Alaska residents pushed for road access to Denali National Park in the early 1930s.

evidence.claim: After World War II, the Alaska Road Commission recommended a Paxson–McKinley Park road; surveys began in 1947 and construction in 1950.
evidence.quote: After the end of the war, the Alaska Road Commission recommended construction of a "Paxson-McKinley Park Road," which began surveys for the project in 1947. Construction began in early 1950

evidence.claim: The highway opened in 1957 as the park’s first road access.
evidence.quote: Opened in 1957, it was the first road access to Denali National Park.

evidence.claim: The original road was commissioned on August 5, 1957; a private vehicle had already traveled its length three days earlier.
evidence.quote: the road was commissioned on August 5, 1957. However, a private vehicle snuck through and drove the length of the highway three days prior.

evidence.claim: Primary access shifted to the Parks Highway in 1971, incorporating the Denali Highway section from Cantwell to the present park entrance.
evidence.quote: Since 1971, primary park access has been via the Parks Highway, which incorporated a section of the Denali Highway from Cantwell to the present-day park entrance.

evidence.claim: Driving west from Tangle Lakes, the road crests at Maclaren Summit and drops into the Maclaren River valley.
evidence.quote: The first 45 miles (72 km) winds through the Amphitheater Mountains, cresting at Maclaren Summit, at 4,086 feet (1,245 m) the second highest road in Alaska. The road then drops down to the Maclaren River Valley

evidence.claim: Beyond the Maclaren crossing it winds through Crazy Notch, follows the foot of the Denali Clearwater Mountains to the Susitna River, then crosses glacial outwash plains toward the Nenana.
evidence.quote: After crossing the Maclaren River, the road winds through the geologically mysterious Crazy Notch and then along the toe of the Denali Clearwater Mountains to the Susitna River. After crossing the Susitna River the road extends across the glacier's outwash plains to the Nenana River

evidence.claim: The final stretch follows that river down to Cantwell and the Parks Highway.
evidence.quote: and then down the Nenana River to Cantwell on the George Parks Highway (Alaska Route 3).

evidence.claim: Streams connect the Tangle Lakes into a 16-mile chain that forms the headwaters of the Delta River.
evidence.quote: are a 16-mile (26 km) long chain of lakes connected by streams in interior Alaska. They form the headwaters for the Delta River.

evidence.claim: Long, Lower, Round and Upper Tangle Lake belong to the chain.
evidence.quote: The Tangle Lakes (Long Tangle Lake, Lower Tangle Lake, Round Tangle Lake, and Upper Tangle Lake)

evidence.claim: At 2,864 feet, the surrounding country is mostly tundra.
evidence.quote: The area around the lakes consists mostly of tundra due to the high elevation (2,864 feet (873 m)).

evidence.claim: Lake trout, burbot and Arctic grayling live in these waters.
evidence.quote: The lakes support many species of fish, including lake trout, burbot, and Arctic grayling.

evidence.claim: The lakes also lie within an extensively studied archaeological landscape: part of the area became a National Register archaeological district in 1971.
evidence.quote: The Tangle Lakes area has been the subject of extensive archaeological exploration.

evidence.claim: The lakes also lie within an extensively studied archaeological landscape: part of the area became a National Register archaeological district in 1971.
evidence.quote: Part of the Tangle Lakes area has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places as an archaeological district in 1971.

evidence.claim: Before 1976, archaeologists had discovered almost 150 sites, evidence of intermittent occupation over a much longer period than the highway’s history.
evidence.quote: Prior to 1976, almost 150 sites had been discovered showing that The Tangle Lakes have been populated intermittently since the settlement of the New World.

evidence.claim: Round Tangle Lake’s BLM campground and boat launch provide the main public access.
evidence.quote: The main public access to the Lakes is from a Bureau of Land Management maintained campground and boat launch at Round Tangle Lake

evidence.claim: Maclaren Summit puts the highway at 4,086 feet after its winding passage through the Amphitheater Mountains.
evidence.quote: The first 45 miles (72 km) winds through the Amphitheater Mountains, cresting at Maclaren Summit, at 4,086 feet

evidence.claim: The BLM’s Maclaren Summit Trail heads north from milepost 39.
evidence.quote: A walk north along The Bureau of Land Management's (BLM) Maclaren Summit Trail (MP 39)

evidence.claim: The highway gives road access to alpine terrain used by breeding birds, including Smith’s longspur, long-tailed jaeger and whimbrel.
evidence.quote: It offers road access to alpine terrain – not that common in Alaska – and, in the brief birding season there, good viewing of a number of alpine breeders, including Arctic Warbler, Smith's Longspur, Long-tailed Jaeger, Whimbrel

evidence.claim: Across its full length, the highway passes through three principal drainage systems: the Copper River, the Tanana/Yukon and the Susitna.
evidence.quote: Along its length, the highway passes through three of the principal river drainages in Interior Alaska: the Copper River drainage, the Tanana/Yukon drainage and the Susitna drainage.

evidence.claim: West of the summit, the road descends into the Maclaren River valley, with views north toward Maclaren Glacier.
evidence.quote: The road then drops down to the Maclaren River Valley with fine views north to Maclaren Glacier.

evidence.claim: It crosses the river before winding onward through Crazy Notch.
evidence.quote: After crossing the Maclaren River, the road winds through the geologically mysterious Crazy Notch

evidence.claim: Winter travel on the highway is by snowmobile or dogsled; it is not a winter automobile route.
evidence.quote: Winter travel on the Denali Highway is exclusively by snowmobile and dogsled.  Automobile travelers are severely discouraged from attempting to traverse the road in winter;

evidence.claim: Cantwell began as an Alaska Railroad flag stop supplying the Valdez Creek mining area, whose community was called Denali.
evidence.quote: The settled town began as a flag stop on the Alaska Railroad. This flagstop supplied the Valdez Creek mining area, which had the name "Denali" for the Valdez Creek community.

evidence.claim: Oley Nicklie, a Native Alaskan, sought railroad work after fur prices fell, and he and his two brothers founded part of the settlement.
evidence.quote: Oley Nicklie, a Native Alaskan, sought work with the railroad after fur prices dropped. He and his two brothers then founded part of the settlement.

evidence.claim: The town sits at the north end of Broad Pass, along Cantwell Creek and the Jack River, tributaries of the north-flowing Nenana.
evidence.quote: It is situated at the north end of Broad Pass, along Cantwell Creek and the Jack River, tributaries of the north-flowing Nenana River.

evidence.claim: Here the Denali Highway reaches its western terminus and meets the Parks Highway.
evidence.quote: It leads from Paxson on the Richardson Highway to Cantwell on the Parks Highway.

evidence.claim: Since 1971, the Parks Highway has provided the primary road access to Denali National Park, incorporating the older highway’s stretch from Cantwell to the park entrance.
evidence.quote: Since 1971, primary park access has been via the Parks Highway, which incorporated a section of the Denali Highway from Cantwell to the present-day park entrance.
